title: Conjecture on the asymptotic of n(2,d)
statement_text: For every $2\leqslant k\leqslant d$, $n(k,d)\leqslant n(k-1,d-1)+n(k,d-1)$ (the 'Pascal Triangle' conjecture). Together with the lower bound $n(2,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, this would imply $\lim_{d\to\infty}\frac{n(2,d)}{d^2}=\frac{1}{2}$.
context_text: A standard box in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a product $K_1\times\cdots\times K_d$ of closed intervals. Two standard boxes $K,L$ are $k$-neighborly if $d-k\leqslant\dim(K\cap L)\leqslant d-1$, and a family of standard boxes is $k$-neighborly if every two of its members are. For $1\leqslant k\leqslant d$, $n(k,d)$ is the maximum size of a $k$-neighborly family of standard boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$; equivalently (Alon), it is the maximum number of vertices of a complete graph whose edges can be covered by $d$ complete bipartite subgraphs so that every edge is covered at least once and at most $k$ times. Zaks proved $n(1,d)=d+1$ via the Graham–Pollak theorem, and $n(d,d)=2^d$. The authors prove $n(k,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^k}{k!}$; for $k=2$ this gives $n(2,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, improving the previous $d^2/4$, while determining the asymptotic order of $n(2,d)$ was noted to be hard by Alon and by Huang–Sudakov. In the final section they pose the Pascal Triangle conjecture, supported by Gurobi computations for $d\leqslant 8$ and by the fact that the analogous inequality holds for the values $\overline{m}(k,d)$ given by their explicit constructions. The Pascal inequality gives $n(2,j)-n(2,j-1)\leqslant j$, hence $n(2,d)\leqslant(d+1)+\binom{d}{2}$, which combined with the lower bound yields the limit $1/2$.
notes: The formal conjecture appears in Section 3 (the final section on total laminations and computational experiments), which is not present in the provided PDF extract. Only the informal forward-reference in the introduction is available; math may be garbled due to PDF source.
paper_title: New bounds on the maximum number of neighborly boxes in R^d

title: Open question on existence of lim n(2,d)/d^2
context_text: A standard box in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a product $K_1\times\cdots\times K_d$ of closed intervals. Two standard boxes $K,L$ are $k$-neighborly if $d-k\leqslant\dim(K\cap L)\leqslant d-1$, and a family of standard boxes is $k$-neighborly if every two of its members are. $n(k,d)$ is the maximum size of a $k$-neighborly family of standard boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$; equivalently (Alon), it is the maximum number of vertices of a complete graph whose edges can be covered by $d$ complete bipartite subgraphs so that every edge is covered at least once and at most $k$ times. The paper proves $n(2,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$ (improving $d^2/4$) and more generally $n(k,d)\geqslant(1-o(1))\frac{d^k}{k!}$. The authors conjecture that for every fixed $k$ the limit $g_k=\lim_{d\to\infty} n(k,d)/d^k$ exists ($g_1=1$ by the Graham–Pollak theorem), and that $g_2=\frac{1}{2}$ would follow from their conjectured Pascal Triangle inequality $n(k,d)\leqslant n(k-1,d-1)+n(k,d-1)$; but they explicitly remark that for $k\geqslant 2$ even the existence of the limit is not known.
notes: Explicitly stated in the introduction: 'as yet we do not even know whether the limit above exists'. PDF source — math notation may be garbled.
